skill_title: Define current, potential difference and EMF and measure them correctly

items.question: What is electric current?
items.expectedAnswer: The rate of flow of charge.
items.explanation: Current is the rate at which charge flows: I = Q/t.
options: The rate of flow of charge.

items.question: How is an ammeter connected in a circuit?
items.explanation: An ammeter measures current and must be connected in series so the current flows through it.

items.question: How is a voltmeter connected in a circuit?
items.explanation: A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in parallel across the component.

items.question: What is potential difference (voltage) across a component?
items.expectedAnswer: The energy transferred per unit charge as it passes through the component.
items.explanation: Potential difference is energy per coulomb transferred between two points.
options: The energy transferred per unit charge as it passes through the component.
The rate of flow of charge.
The total charge in the circuit.

items.question: What is the EMF of a cell?
items.expectedAnswer: The total energy supplied per unit charge by the cell.
items.explanation: EMF is the energy per coulomb provided by the source to the charges.
options: The total energy supplied per unit charge by the cell.

items.question: Which equation relates charge, current and time?
items.explanation: Charge = current × time: Q = It.

items.question: In what unit is electric current measured?
items.explanation: Current is measured in amperes (A).

items.question: A current of 2 A flows for 5 s. How much charge passes a point?
In what unit is potential difference measured?
items.explanation: Potential difference is measured in volts (V).

items.question: A charge of 12 C flows past a point in 4 s. What is the current?
An ammeter is mistakenly connected in parallel across a resistor. What is the likely problem?
items.expectedAnswer: It has very low resistance, so it short-circuits the resistor and a large current may flow.
items.explanation: Ammeters have very low resistance and must be in series; in parallel they short the component.
options: It will read the correct current.
It has very low resistance, so it short-circuits the resistor and a large current may flow.
It will read the potential difference instead.

items.question: A voltmeter is mistakenly connected in series. What is the likely problem?
items.expectedAnswer: Its very high resistance almost stops the current, so the circuit barely works.
items.explanation: Voltmeters have very high resistance and must be in parallel; in series they block the current.
options: It will read the correct voltage.
It will read the current instead.
Its very high resistance almost stops the current, so the circuit barely works.

items.question: A current of 0.5 A flows through a lamp for 2 minutes. How much charge passes through it?
items.explanation: Convert time: 2 min = 120 s. Q = It = 0.5 × 120 = 60 C.

items.question: How much charge flows when a current of 3 A is maintained for 0.5 minutes?
Why is EMF usually slightly larger than the terminal voltage of a real battery when current flows?
items.expectedAnswer: Some energy per coulomb is used inside the battery's own (internal) resistance.
items.explanation: A real cell has internal resistance, so the terminal voltage is the EMF minus the 'lost volts' inside.
options: EMF is always smaller than terminal voltage.
Terminal voltage includes the EMF twice.
Some energy per coulomb is used inside the battery's own (internal) resistance.

items.question: A battery delivers 30 J of energy to every 2 C of charge passing through it. What is its EMF?
items.explanation: EMF = energy per charge = 30/2 = 15 V (J per C).

items.question: If 24 J of energy is transferred by 4 C of charge passing through a resistor, what is the potential difference across it?
items.explanation: V = energy/charge = 24/4 = 6 V.

items.question: What does it mean physically that the current is the same everywhere in a simple series circuit?
items.expectedAnswer: Charge is not used up; the same rate of flow passes every component.
items.explanation: Charge is conserved, so the same current flows through each series component (charge is not consumed).
options: The charge is shared out and reduces along the circuit.
Charge is not used up; the same rate of flow passes every component.

items.question: A current of 5 A flows for 4 s. The same charge then flows in 2 s through another wire. What is the current in the second wire?
items.explanation: Charge Q = It = 5 × 4 = 20 C. In the second wire I = Q/t = 20/2 = 10 A.

items.question: Which instrument arrangement correctly measures both the current through and the voltage across a single resistor?
items.expectedAnswer: Ammeter in series with the resistor; voltmeter in parallel across it.
items.explanation: Current needs the ammeter in series; voltage needs the voltmeter in parallel across the resistor.
options: Ammeter in parallel; voltmeter in series.
Ammeter in series with the resistor; voltmeter in parallel across it.
Both in series with the resistor.
